analysis.one_liner: Sunsets the entire federal tax code to force a simpler, low-rate replacement.
analysis.headline: Backed by 122 cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote and died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would shut off every tax imposed by the federal tax code after 2017 — the individual income tax, the corporate tax, and the estate tax — keeping only Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes. It writes no replacement: it merely declares that a new system should be simple and fair, apply "a low rate to all Americans," and be approved by Congress by July 4, 2017. Changing the termination date would take a two-thirds vote of each chamber. If Congress failed to agree on a new system in time, the federal government would lose most of its revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and investors would gain the most: the progressive income tax, taxes on capital gains and dividends, and the estate tax would all end, and the declared replacement standard is a single low rate with no tax on savings and investment. Supporters of a flat tax or a national sales tax would gain a forcing mechanism, since the old code must die whether or not a new one is ready. Every taxpayer who finds filing costly and complicated would gain if the promised simpler system actually materialized.

how_it_helps.text: Sunsets every tax imposed by the Internal Revenue Code after 2017 — the individual income tax, corporate tax, and estate tax — keeping only Social Security (FICA), self-employment, and railroad retirement payroll taxes.

Declares that the replacement system should be simple and fair: a low rate for all Americans, tax relief for working Americans, stronger taxpayer rights, no tax penalty on saving and investment, economic growth, and no marriage penalty.
Declares that a new tax system should be approved by Congress in final form by July 4, 2017, to allow an orderly transition.
Requires a two-thirds vote in each chamber to change the termination date, locking the sunset in place.

analysis.who_pays: Working and middle-income households would bear the shift: Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes would continue as they are, while replacing a progressive code with "a low rate" for everyone would cut taxes most, in dollars, at the top and leave the load relatively heavier further down. And if Congress missed the non-binding deadline for a replacement, the government would lose the income taxes that supply most of its funding, forcing deep spending cuts or large new borrowing.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the entire revenue system before any replacement exists. The principles for the new system and the July 2017 deadline are declarations, not binding requirements, so nothing in the bill forces Congress to actually pass a new tax law. If no replacement cleared Congress in time, the federal government would lose the individual and corporate income taxes that supply most of its revenue.

A replacement built on 'a low rate to all Americans' would replace a progressive income tax — under which high earners pay a larger share of their income — with a flatter structure that cuts taxes most at the top. Payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare, which fall on wages, would continue unchanged.

Changing the termination date would require a two-thirds vote of members voting in each chamber, and the bill writes that requirement into each chamber's own rules — making it extremely difficult to delay or fix the sunset once enacted.

Nearly five years of uncertainty about the most fundamental rules in the economy — created by a fixed sunset date with an unspecified replacement — would complicate planning for households, businesses, and markets the entire time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — a simpler, fairer tax code — addresses a real cost ordinary households bear every year in time and money. But the design is a gamble: it kills the entire revenue system before a replacement is written, makes both the replacement principles and the approval deadline non-binding declarations, and locks the sunset behind a two-thirds vote. Its own standard of "a low rate to all Americans" points toward a flatter tax that cuts bills most at the top, while the payroll taxes that fall on wages continue untouched. As written, the risks to working households outweigh the promised simplification — though in practice the bill never advanced far enough for any of this to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Goodlatte introduced the bill on January 23, 2013, and it was referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee and, for the two-thirds-vote provision, to the Rules Committee.
122 members cosponsored the bill: 120 Republicans and 2 Democrats.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
The bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, today's progressive income tax stayed in place, so ordinary households were spared a shift toward a low-rate system whose benefits would concentrate at the top — while high earners and investors remain subject to the current code and the tax-preparation industry keeps its complex market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working households kept the existing tax code.

for.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tax Code Termination Act on January 23, 2013, with original cosponsors including members of House leadership and committee chairmen.

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in his committee from the day of referral until the Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or vote; its only recorded action was the January 23, 2013 referral.

against.name: House Rules Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over floor procedure
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on dual referral — the two-thirds-vote provision falls under its jurisdiction — and never considered it.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was almost entirely Republican — 120 of 233 House Republicans versus 2 of 201 House Democrats — but the bill never came to a vote, and it was the Republican-chaired Ways and Means Committee that let it die.

industries.note: Ending the progressive income tax, the taxation of capital gains and dividends, and the estate tax — with a declared replacement of 'a low rate' and no tax on savings and investment — would cut tax bills most at the top, while payroll taxes on wages continue unchanged.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and compliance industry (software, preparers, accountants)
industries.note: A tax code rebuilt around simplicity would shrink demand for tax software, preparers, and tax lawyers, whose market is the complexity of the current code. Until a simpler system actually replaced it, the old code — and their business — would survive.
